extracted.intended_audience: citizens, delegates, and policymakers considering the structure and provisions of a federal legislature (ratifiers of the U.S. Constitution / constitutional designers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and normative criteria for designing the composition, apportionment, term length, and election frequency of a federal House of Representatives (arguments for biennial elections, apportionment rules including the three-fifths compromise, and size of the chamber).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of elections / term length (biennial vs annual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Biennial elections are defended as safe to the liberty of the people and appropriate for the federal government; the proverb 'where annual elections end, tyranny begins' is questioned and annual elections are argued to be unnecessary for a government limited by a paramount Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments and examples: varied election periods among States (half-yearly to septennial) show no necessary correlation between frequency and good government; where a constitution is paramount, biennial elections fixed by that constitution provide at least as much security (and likely more) than annual elections subject to change. Practical reasons for two-year terms are developed elsewhere (knowledge acquisition, travel, contesting returns, stability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of power to duration of office
rubrics_metrics.description: The duration of political power should bear an inverse relation to the extent of the power: 'where no other circumstances affect the case, the greater the power is, the shorter ought to be its duration; and, conversely, the smaller the power, the more safely may its duration be protracted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to the federal legislature: because the federal House possesses only part of supreme legislative authority (unlike the British Parliament), longer terms (biennial) are acceptable and safe. This principle is used to justify the proposed term length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Period of service should match required legislative knowledge/experience
rubrics_metrics.description: A competent legislator must have upright intention, sound judgment, and a certain degree of knowledge; the period of service ought to bear some proportion to the extent of practical knowledge requisite to perform the service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For federal legislators this includes knowledge of varied state laws, general affairs across many states, foreign commerce and treaties, the law of nations, militia regulations, and tax accommodations. Two-year terms better enable acquisition of such practical experience than one-year terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collateral oversight by State legislatures reduces need for very frequent elections
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal legislature will be watched and controlled by the several collateral (state) legislatures in a way that other legislative bodies are not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of this additional oversight and the limited scope of federal powers, the people’s interests are doubly watched — lessening the necessity of very frequent elections to safeguard liberties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment based on population (including treatment of slaves)
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation is to be regulated by a census of inhabitants; whether slaves should be included is debated, and the Constitution adopts a compromising view counting slaves as part-person, part-property (the Three-Fifths compromise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: slaves possess a mixed legal character (in some respects persons, in others property); the Constitution treats them as inhabitants but 'debased by servitude' and counts them in the federal census as three-fifths of a person. Also: states decide suffrage qualifications internally; the federal rule determines aggregate apportionment while states decide who chooses the allotted representatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation should give some regard to property/wealth as well as persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Government is instituted for protection of both persons and property; representation should, therefore, pay some attention to property and relative wealth among States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since a State (unlike an individual) cannot influence another State by private standing, the comparative wealth and importance of States should be reflected by proportionate representation so that richer/more important States obtain due influence in the federal legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use same rule for apportionment of representation and direct taxation to balance incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Extending the same rule (population) to both representation and direct taxation will produce opposite incentives that check one another and encourage accurate census reporting by States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If representation alone used the rule, States would over-report inhabitants; if taxation alone, they would under-report. Applying the rule to both creates countervailing interests that promote impartiality and cooperation with the census.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of representatives must balance effective deliberation and avoidance of mob rule
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a certain minimum number to secure free consultation and discussion and guard against improper combinations, but a limit should prevent confusion and intemperance from a multitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numeric plan in the Constitution: initial House of 65, a census within three years permitting increase to one representative per 30,000 inhabitants and decennial reapportionment thereafter. Projections indicate growth to hundreds over decades; fears about smallness are mitigated by these increases and by the present temper and political institutions of the people and States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical logistical considerations (travel, distance) favor longer terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The distance many representatives must travel and the arrangements required make very short terms (e.g., one year) a stronger disincentive to public service among fit men than longer terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-year terms reduce the relative burden of travel and associated arrangements, encouraging qualified persons to serve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of spurious or illegitimate elections is greater under very frequent elections
rubrics_metrics.description: In assemblies that hold only one session per year, spurious elections cannot be investigated and annulled in time to have due effect; an illegitimate member may hold a seat long enough to serve wrongful purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer terms reduce the incentive to obtain seats by unlawful means because the time for adjudication and removal will be more adequate and the immediate benefits to the wrongdoer correspondingly reduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion of experienced vs new members affects vulnerability to corruption/influence
rubrics_metrics.description: A few members will possess superior talents and, by frequent reelection, become long-standing masters of public business; a greater proportion of new, less informed members makes the body more apt to fall into snares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer terms and the prospect of reelection foster accumulation of experience; institutional relations (e.g., between House and Senate) and the presence of experienced members reduce susceptibility to improper influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal acts take effect by federal majority so representation must reflect States' relative importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the proposed Constitution, federal acts will take effect without necessary intervention of the States; each representative’s vote has equal legal efficacy, so the numerical share of representation should reflect the comparative wealth and importance of States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because votes will be legally equal in effect, larger or wealthier States should receive proportionally greater representation to secure any legitimate advantage that their relative wealth and weight might entitle them to in the federal government (contrasting with confederacies where state votes and subsequent voluntary state action conveyed unequal influence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Numeric and procedural design details: initial size, census timing, apportionment ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific constitutional provisions cited: House initially 65 members; a census within three years; thereafter the ratio of one representative per 30,000 may be used and reapportionment every ten years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedural details are advanced as practical measures to allow growth and to address concerns about smallness of the initial body; they provide a concrete schedule for increasing representation in line with population growth.
